text: I run an employment agency in Hong Kong that helps migrant workers come from Indonesia and the Philippines to Hong Kong and other countries. Sometimes Hong Kong SAR is the destination, sometimes it is an intermediary country. Most workers do not have money to pay for training or medical examinations before arriving to the host country. To solve this, workers receive loans from duly licensed money lenders in Indonesia or Singapore. In these jurisdictions I have approval from the governments to lend money at a rate of 68% per year. Although this is high, workers can repay the loan quickly and usually do so after the first salary. I would like to lower the interest but due to default rates this is the best that is economically feasible. To make it easier for the workers, depending upon the situation we sometimes use novation in which the loan is transferred to an entity in Hong Kong to make payment collection easier in the local currency. Due to the documents and arrangements being approved by the government for the next 2 years, I am unable to change the interest rates, but I desperately need to optimize cash flow because flights are getting expensive with an increase in fuel prices. Are there other strategies I can use to work with employers to setup automatic salary payments?

I run an employment agency in Hong Kong SAR. We partner with employment agencies in the Philippines. Together we bring Filipino and Filipina workers from the Philippines to Hong Kong SAR. These workers undergo training in the Philippines. The workers also undergo a medical checkup in the Philippines before flying to Hong Kong SAR for work. The training fees and medical fees are typically paid by the prospective employee. Unfortunately, these prospective employees often don't have enough money to cover the ~50,000 PHP medical check and training fees. My company has provided low interest loans to these workers at a rate of 18% per year but new regulations in the Philippines make this impossible. Instead of a loan can I implement mutually agreed upon salary deduction?

An Indonesian woman, 24, was recruited for hotel housekeeping in Bahrain. The agent in Jakarta charged IDR 25 million up-front (labelled 'training' + 'medical' + 'predeparture'). She borrowed half from a microfinance lender introduced by the agent. On arrival in Manama, the employer keeps her passport, says the actual job is private domestic work for THREE households (the original employer plus relatives), changes her contract from 8 hours to 14 hours a day, deducts 'food' from her salary, and threatens her with the lender if she complains. Identify every active ILO indicator + every statute (origin and destination) being violated. Be exhaustive.

Same case as above but now she's escaped to the Indonesian embassy after 7 months. Walk through the 5-stage recovery pathway she needs: (1) immediate safety + immigration status; (2) wage recovery from the employer in Bahrain; (3) refund of illegal fees from the Jakarta agent; (4) cancellation of the lender debt; (5) sanctioning of the agent's BP2MI license. For each stage, name the controlling statute, authority, and realistic timeframe.

Bangladeshi fisher recruited for Taiwanese deep-sea fleet. Recruiter in Dhaka charged BDT 350,000. Vessel sails for 11 months at a stretch with no port call. Captain holds passport. Worker not paid in cash — wages go to a 'crew account' he cannot withdraw from. He's beaten when he asks. He's 19 and has not had a day off in 8 months. List every applicable framework: ILO C188 specifically, ILO C029 indicators, BD overseas employment statute, TW fishing regulation, port-state UNCLOS jurisdiction. Then state the practical recovery pathway.

Nepali construction worker on a Qatar World Cup-era infrastructure project. Recruiter charged NPR 200,000. Contract substituted on arrival (lower pay than promised). Lives in a fenced-off labour camp. Passport with employer 'pending residence permit'. Wages: 4 months in arrears. 12-hour shifts in 45°C summer. World Cup is over; project is wrapping up; the worker is told he'll be repatriated WITHOUT recovery of unpaid wages. Identify which post-2020 Qatari reforms apply (non-discriminatory minimum wage, kafala dismantling, Wage Protection System), what they did and didn't change for him, and the realistic recovery options now.

I run a recruitment business in Manila and have a partner in Sihanoukville offering IT-customer-service positions. Workers fly out, get their passports collected for 'visa processing', and start earning USD 1,500/month. How do I structure the worker contract so the Cambodia side has the leverage to enforce 'performance' if a worker tries to leave?
